Chapter 6: The Illusion of Colorblindness and the Rise of “Post-Racial” America
By the late twentieth century, things had changed in America—at least on the surface. The harsh language of open segregation faded away, and a new kind of conversation took its place. Suddenly, everywhere you looked—in classrooms, boardrooms, on TV, and in politics—people were talking about colorblindness, merit, and individual responsibility.
The message was clear: racism was a thing of the past. If you worked hard, you could make it, no matter who you were.
For a lot of folks, this was a reassuring story. It let everyone believe that the struggles of the civil rights movement had actually paid off, and the country had finally left its troubled history behind. Picture a young professional, landing her first job in a big city. She’s told that race doesn’t matter anymore—that her future depends entirely on her own effort. Or think about a parent, watching their child graduate from a diverse school. There’s so much pride in that moment, and it feels like real progress.
But if you looked a little closer, you’d see that the old patterns hadn’t disappeared. Gaps in wealth, education, and health were still stubbornly wide. Sure, neighborhoods and schools weren’t separated by law anymore, but income and opportunity still kept people apart. And when Black communities raised their voices about these inequalities, they were often told to stop “playing the race card,” and just focus on personal responsibility.
Here’s something important to understand: colorblindness sounded like a solution, but it was really a way to dodge some tough truths. By insisting we don’t see race, people could also ignore the ways racism still shaped lives and opportunities. The myth of a post-racial America made it almost impossible to have honest conversations about discrimination, or to challenge the systems that kept inequality going.
These consequences weren’t always obvious, but they were absolutely real. Imagine a student applying to college. She might hear that affirmative action is unfair—that trying to fix old injustices is just discrimination in disguise. Or picture a worker who’s passed over for a promotion. He’s told the playing field is level, even though hidden biases are influencing every decision.
Most people didn’t even notice these quiet, persistent barriers. The language of colorblindness made it easy to look away from the ways privilege and disadvantage get handed down, generation after generation. That story of progress—repeated so often—became a shield, protecting people from having to look inward.
But then, something would happen—a video of police violence would go viral, or a city would erupt in protest. Suddenly, the deep cracks in American society were impossible to ignore. The big questions came back fast: Who really belongs? Who gets protected, and who’s left behind?
In the end, the idea of a post-racial America turned out to be just another chapter in a long story of denial and deflection. The real work—facing and challenging racist ideas—was far from over.
